newsitem.title: DUBAI: U.S. hits Iraq to secure wider no-fly zone.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hits Iraq to secure wider no-fly zone.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday fired missiles at Iraqi surface-to-air missile sites and air defence installations to secure an expanded and safer no-fly zone in the south of the country.

The United States said four navy vessels fired 17 Tomahawk missiles at air "defence targets" in the south, a day after it had launched 27 of the $1.2 million precision weapons at similar targets in the south.

Western military sources said the repeat attack targeted surface-to-air missile sites, radars and other command, control and communications (C3) centres to facilitate the enforcement of an expanded zone in the south.

One said Washington was seeking "to clean" southern Iraq of military facilities which could threaten American, French and British warplanes that start at noon on Wednesday (0800 GMT) to enforce the new zone.

"The Americans have good data and intelligence on Iraqi (military) positions in the whole southern area," said an Arab military expert, expressing the view that most of the missiles had probably achieved their aim.

Wednesday's missile launches started shortly after 2:50 a.m. (2350 GMT Tuesday) in a "restrike of targets (attacked on Tuesday) to make sure we made the best job," a U.S. military spokesman in the Gulf told Reuters.

Iraqi President Saddam Hussein on Tuesday called on his air defence and air force units to ignore the wider zone, up to the 33rd parallel on the outskirts of Baghdad, and even the original 32nd parallel no-fly zone which was set up following his defeat in the 1991 Gulf War.
The zone is also a "no-drive" one for Iraqi troops, banning Baghdad from sending added forces by land into the Shiite Moslem dominated south other than units orginally deployed in the area.
Washington says the wider zone is aimed at further restricting Iraq's ability to pose a threat to neighbours.

Saddam still commands one of the region's largest war machines with a 400,000-man force, 2,200 tanks after losing 2,600 in the war and a variety of fixed-wing aircraft -- 150 to 350 of which are operational -- including Russian MiGs, Sukhois and bombers.
The United States has about 20,000 troops deployed in and around the Gulf backed by more than 300 warplanes and military hardware stored in Gulf Arab states.
The latest confrontation with Iraq was triggered by Saddam's sending of troops on Saturday into Iraq's Kurdish north in support of one Kurdish faction against a rival group.
The Pentagon and White House said the repeat strike was authorised by President Bill Clinton and was made against a number of targets that were not completely damaged in the earlier attack.
